title: Behavioural: why-I-left, mistake, conflict, feedback and your questions
seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic JEE-style quizzes for the backend and AI-engineering interview roadmap: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code writing, plus multi-correct questions. Language core, concurrency, DSA, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, LLM and agent engineering.
description: Framing why you are leaving and why this company, telling mistake, conflict and feedback stories, and asking the interviewer good questions. Scenario-judgement style: pick the strongest answer or the statement that weakens a story.
source: Amazon Leadership Principles and interview guide (aboutamazon.com); Harvard Business Review on behavioural interviewing; Cracking the Coding Interview (behavioural chapter); common interview-prep guides on STAR, exit reasons and questions to ask

questions.prompt: You plan a 3-minute (180 s) answer: 30 s for Situation and Task together, and 30 s for the Result. How many seconds remain for the Action?
questions.explanation: 180 - 30 - 30 = 120 s, about two thirds of the answer. Timing varies, but Action should dominate.

questions.prompt: You want to cover all 16 Amazon Leadership Principles, and each story can credibly cover at most 3 distinct principles. What is the minimum number of stories?
questions.explanation: ceil(16 / 3) = 6. In practice prepare 8 to 10 so you can pick a different story for a repeat question in the same loop.

questions.prompt: Write one thoughtful question to ask an engineering interviewer about how the team runs its services in production (for example on-call, incidents or operational ownership).
questions.model: How does the team handle on-call and what changes after a serious incident, for example post-incident reviews and follow-up actions?
questions.explanation: Free-text: any open, specific question about operations passes. Good questions show curiosity about how work really happens, not about perks.

questions.prompt: Write a two-sentence answer to "Why are you leaving your current job?" that is forward-looking and does not criticise your employer. Mention what you are looking for.

checks.label: says what you are looking for

questions.model: I have enjoyed building and owning backend services, and I have learned a lot there. I am now looking for larger-scale distributed systems problems and broader ownership, which is why this role excites me.
questions.explanation: Keep it brief, truthful, positive and about the future. Pull toward something, rather than pushing away from something.

questions.prompt: Asked "Why do you want to work here?", which answer is strongest?

options.text: Link a specific company problem to your own experience.
options.why: Right: specific and mutual; it shows research and fit.

options.text: Say that the compensation and the brand name are the main reasons you applied to this particular role.
options.why: Honest perhaps, but it says nothing about fit or motivation.

options.text: Say that a friend told you it is a good place and that you want to switch jobs soon.
options.why: Vague and second-hand; it does not show your own reasons.

options.text: Say you are open to any team and will take whatever the company needs right now.
options.why: Lack of direction reads as low motivation.

questions.explanation: Prepare two or three concrete reasons from product, scale, engineering culture or mission, each tied to something you have done.

options.text: Understood their constraint, agreed on data, committed.
options.why: Right: empathy, data and commitment show maturity.

options.text: Escalated to the manager straight away so that a decision could be made without wasting my own time.
options.why: Skipping direct conversation signals poor conflict skills.

options.text: Waited for the other person to leave the project so that the disagreement resolved itself over time.
options.why: Avoidance resolves nothing.

options.text: Won the argument by presenting my own opinion repeatedly in meetings until the group gave in.
options.why: Persistence without data or listening is not influence.

questions.explanation: Show you disagreed respectfully, used data and then supported the decision. The Result should include the working relationship, not only the code.

questions.prompt: Which feedback story shows coachability best?

options.text: Specific feedback, my change, and the later measured result.
options.why: Right: concrete input, concrete change, measurable effect.

options.text: Feedback that I was too much of a perfectionist, which I treat as a strength and still handle in exactly the same way.
options.why: No change and no evidence of learning.

options.text: Feedback that I disagreed with and ignored because the reviewer lacked context on the project.
options.why: Dismissing feedback signals low coachability.

options.text: General praise from my manager on my annual review, which I was happy to receive from the team.
options.why: Praise is not developmental feedback.

questions.explanation: Choose real, developmental feedback, show that you asked clarifying questions, changed behaviour and followed up.

questions.prompt: Which statements weaken a STAR story? Select all that apply.

options.text: "We did a lot of work and it went well in the end."
options.why: Right: vague, no individual role, no result.

options.text: "The release fixed things, though I never checked whether the numbers actually improved."
options.why: Right: no measured result.

options.text: "The tester kept missing bugs, which is why the release slipped."
options.why: Right: blaming others sounds defensive.

options.text: "Looking back I would add a canary step, and I added it the following sprint."
options.why: This strengthens the story by showing learning.

questions.explanation: Specific I-statements, numbers, trade-offs considered and lessons applied make a story credible.

questions.prompt: Which questions are good to ask the interviewer? Select all that apply.

options.text: What does success look like in the first six months?
options.why: Right: shows you care about impact.

options.text: How does the team decide between shipping fast and paying down technical debt?
options.why: Right: reveals engineering culture and shows judgement.

options.text: How soon can I be promoted after joining?
options.why: Premature and focused only on yourself.

options.text: What does your company do?
options.why: Basic research you should have done beforehand.

questions.explanation: Ask about the work, the team, the challenges and how you will be measured. Avoid questions answered on the careers page.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: A failure story should end with what you changed afterwards.
questions.reason: Interviewers use failure stories to judge ownership and whether you learn from mistakes.

whys.a: Correct: the change is the evidence of learning, which is what the interviewer is assessing.

questions.explanation: The strongest endings are systemic: a test, a checklist, an alert or a changed process.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: Admitting a real mistake will always eliminate you from an Amazon interview loop.
questions.reason: Interviewers look for ownership and learning, which a good failure story demonstrates.

whys.c: R is true, so this option is wrong.
whys.d: Correct: A is false and R is true; a candid, well-handled mistake is what they are looking for, whereas evading is the red flag.

questions.explanation: Pick a real failure with moderate stakes and take responsibility.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: Asking good questions at the end of an interview helps show genuine interest in the role.
questions.reason: You should ask nothing, because questions waste the interviewer's time.

whys.a: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
whys.c: Correct: A is true; R is false, since interviewers expect and value thoughtful questions.

questions.explanation: Prepare three or four questions per round and adapt them to the interviewer's role.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: Criticising a former employer in an interview damages your credibility.
questions.reason: Behavioural questions are usually open-ended rather than yes/no.

whys.a: R is true but unrelated to why criticism hurts.
whys.b: Correct: both are true and independent; the interviewer infers how you might speak about them later.

questions.explanation: Frame reasons positively: scope, scale, learning, mission.

questions.prompt: Match each story type to what the interviewer is mainly testing.

right.text: Respectful disagreement, data use and commitment
Curiosity and what you value in a team

questions.explanation: Knowing what each question probes tells you what to emphasise.

questions.text: In a conflict story show that you {1} the other person's constraints, used {2} rather than opinion, and {3} to the final decision.
questions.explanation: Understanding, evidence and commitment are the three beats of a mature conflict story.

questions.prompt: True or false: you may reuse one strong story for different questions if you emphasise different actions each time.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: this is normal; just avoid repeating the identical story in the same interview loop when you have alternatives.

options.text: False
options.why: Reuse is fine when the emphasis changes.

questions.explanation: Prepare more stories than principles so a repeated question gets a fresh example.

questions.prompt: Asked 'What is your greatest weakness?', which answer is strongest?

options.text: A real, non-critical weakness, the concrete steps you took on it, and visible progress.
options.why: Right: honesty plus a working improvement plan shows self-awareness.

options.text: 'I am a perfectionist', followed by an explanation that this is really a strength for the team.
options.why: A disguised strength sounds rehearsed and avoids the question.

options.text: A weakness that is central to the job, such as 'I find debugging production issues stressful'.
options.why: A core-skill weakness without a plan makes the interviewer doubt the fit.

options.text: 'I do not really have weaknesses that affect my work', since you track your performance closely.
options.why: Claiming none signals low self-awareness, which interviewers read as a risk.

questions.explanation: Pick something genuinely improvable (for example delegating, or writing design docs earlier), say what you changed, and give evidence it worked.

questions.prompt: Asked about a time you had to decide with incomplete data, which answer shows the most mature judgement?

options.text: State the assumptions, pick a reversible step, set a metric and a checkpoint, then adjust.
options.why: Right: it shows bias for action with a safety net and a learning loop.

options.text: Wait until the missing data arrives, because acting on partial information is always irresponsible.
options.why: Always waiting is the opposite of bias for action when decisions are reversible.

options.text: Make the call alone and quietly, because asking for input would show a lack of confidence.
options.why: Skipping stakeholders hides risk and weakens trust.

options.text: Escalate to the manager immediately and implement whichever option they choose, without analysis.
options.why: Escalating with no analysis shows no ownership of the decision.

questions.explanation: Interviewers map this to Bias for Action and Are Right, A Lot. Name what you did not know, how you reduced the risk, and what you measured afterwards.
